draft.title: Compound and complex sentences
card: A clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb. A main clause makes sense on its own: "The bus was late."
two main clauses joined by a word such as and, but or so. "The bus was late, but Ravi still made it."
a main clause plus a dependent clause. A dependent clause cannot stand alone. It often starts with a word such as because, although or when.
"Ravi ran, because the bus was late." Here "because the bus was late" is dependent. It needs the main clause to make sense.
draft.remember: Compound sentences join equal main clauses. Complex sentences add a dependent clause.

a.q: Which of these is a complex sentence?
opts: Mia stayed inside because it was raining
Mia stayed inside, and she read a book
Mia stayed inside, but Leo went out
Mia stayed inside, so she read a book
a.why: "Because it was raining" is a dependent clause. It cannot stand alone, so the sentence is complex. The other three join two main clauses, which makes them compound.
a.clue: Look for a clause that cannot stand alone.

opts: The dog barked, and the cat hid under the bed
The dog barked when the cat walked past it
Although the dog barked, the cat stayed calm
The cat hid because the dog barked loudly
b.why: Both parts of the first sentence can stand alone, and and joins them. The others each have a dependent clause beginning with when, although or because. The sentence starting with although is tempting, but "Although the dog barked" cannot stand alone.
b.clue: Check whether each part could be its own sentence.

a.best: Mia stayed inside because it was raining

b.best: The dog barked, and the cat hid under the bed

problems.detail: Why (b) says 'Both parts of the first sentence can stand alone', but the options are shown in random order, so 'the first sentence' may not be the right answer. Here the first option is the 'Although' sentence, which is dependent-led. Name the sentence instead of its position.

The right option is the only one with no comma. The three compound options all use ', but', ', so' and ', and'. A student could pick the answer from punctuation alone, without knowing what a dependent clause is.

The example 'Ravi ran, because the bus was late.' puts a comma before 'because'. When a dependent clause follows the main clause, it usually takes no comma. This also clashes with question a's 'Mia stayed inside because it was raining' and could confuse Year 7 students about punctuation.

check.summary: Both answers are clear and correct, but Why (b) refers to 'the first sentence' even though option order is random. The right option in question a also stands out as the only one without a comma, and the card's example puts an unusual comma before 'because'.
